summary: Tractate Yoma opens with the Mishnah's rule that seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is separated from his home to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and another kohen is prepared in case he becomes disqualified; Rabbi Yehuda wants another wife prepared too, lest his wife die, since 'his house' in the verse means his wife, but the Sages answer that if so there is no end to the matter. The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah taught elsewhere: the kohen who burns the parah adumah is likewise separated seven days beforehand, to the chamber facing the Bira to the northeast, called the Chamber of the Stone House; the Gemara explains the name: all the parah's acts were done with dung, stone, and earth vessels. The reason for those vessels is that a tevul yom is fit for the parah (they would make the kohen tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees who required sunset), so the Sages required vessels that cannot become impure, so that people would not treat the parah lightly. The chamber is in the northeast as a distinguishing sign: the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting. Rabbi Yochanan explains 'Bira' as a specific place on the Temple Mount, and Reish Lakish as the whole Temple. Finally, Rabbi Yochanan derives both separations from the verse 'as was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you' (which Rashi places at the milu'im, the inauguration): 'to do' is the parah and 'to atone' is Yom Kippur. When the Gemara asks why the whole verse should not refer to Yom Kippur, it answers with a verbal analogy on 'tzivah' linking the verse to the parah statute. The daf ends as the Gemara begins a further challenge ('ve'eima'), which continues on the next daf.

display.title: Why dung, stone, and earth vessels? Balancing the tvul yom leniency
display.oneLine: Because a tvul yom is fit to burn the parah, as shown by the practice of making the kohen tamei and immersing him to refute the Sadducees, the Sages required vessels that cannot become tamei, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara explains why the parah's service used only dung, stone, and earth vessels. A tvul yom is fit to perform the parah, as a Mishnah shows: the kohen was made tamei and immersed, to refute the Sadducees, who held that it could be done only by one whose sun had set. Because of that leniency, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity, so that people would not come to treat the parah lightly.
display.whats: Why were all the parah's acts done with dung, stone, and earth vessels? Because a tvul yom, one who immersed today and whose sun has not yet set, is fit to perform the parah. A Mishnah shows it: they would make the kohen who burns the parah tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees, who said it was done only by those whose sun had set. Since the parah is lenient in this respect, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity at all, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

display.title: Why was the chamber placed in the northeast?
display.oneLine: The Sages placed the chamber in the northeast as a distinguishing sign: the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse says 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' (which Rashi explains as facing the Sanctuary entrance, to the east).
display.shortSummary: The Gemara asks why the chamber was to the northeast. Since the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and of it is written 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting', the Sages instituted a northeast chamber so that it would have a distinguishing sign (heikher). Rashi explains that the kohen sprinkles toward the Sanctuary entrance, on the east, and that the parah itself was not slaughtered in the north.

Rashi explains that 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' means the kohen sprinkles toward the Sanctuary entrance, on the east, and that the sign shows the kohen was separated there for the parah.

display.title: What does 'bira' mean? Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish
display.oneLine: Rabbi Yochanan says 'bira' was a specific named spot on the Temple Mount; Reish Lakish says the whole Temple is called Bira, citing the verse 'the Bira which I prepared'.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara asks what 'bira' is. Rabbi Yochanan holds it was a specific named location on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish holds that the whole Temple is called Bira, citing the verse 'the Bira which I prepared' (Rashi: David's words in Chronicles).
display.whats: The Gemara asks what 'bira' is. Rabbi Yochanan: it was a specific place on the Temple Mount with that name. Reish Lakish: the whole Temple is called Bira, as it says 'the Bira which I prepared', which Rashi explains as David's words in Chronicles about the Temple.

learning.learnerQuestion: Is 'bira' a specific spot on the Temple Mount, or a term for the whole Temple?

learning.coreMove: Reish Lakish supports his view with the verse 'the Bira which I prepared' (Rashi: David's words in Chronicles about the Temple).
learning.resolution: The dispute is left unresolved here; both views are preserved.

takeaway.text: The Gemara records two definitions of Bira without deciding: a specific place on the Temple Mount (Rabbi Yochanan) or the whole Mikdash (Reish Lakish).

reasoningPattern.notes: Two Amoraim define the word Bira; Reish Lakish cites a verse, and the Gemara does not decide.

display.title: Source for the seven-day separation: gezerah shavah from Leviticus 8
display.oneLine: Rabbi Yochanan derives both seven-day separations from Leviticus 8:34: 'to do' for the parah, 'to atone' for Yom Kippur; a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' ties the verse to the parah statute, and the discussion continues on the next amud.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara asks where the seven-day separation comes from. Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (Rashi: said at the milu'im, the inauguration): 'as was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you.' 'To do' is read as the parah adumah; 'to atone' is read as Yom Kippur. The whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since a parah does not atone. When the Gemara suggests that the whole verse refers to Yom Kippur, it answers with a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): as there it is the parah, so here it is the parah, and as here there is separation, so there the parah requires separation. The discussion continues on the next amud.
display.whats: The Gemara asks: where does the Torah mandate the seven-day separation at all? Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (Rashi: said at the milu'im, the inauguration): 'as was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you.' 'To do' refers to the parah adumah and 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. Granted, the whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since 'to atone' is written and a parah is not a matter of atonement; but say it all refers to Yom Kippur? The Gemara answers with a gezerah shavah on 'commanded/commanded' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): just as the parah verse there refers to the parah, so too 'commanded' here refers to the parah; and just as here there is separation, so too there, regarding the parah, separation is required. The discussion continues on the next amud.
display.hint: Once 'to atone' rules out reading the whole verse as the parah alone, how does the Gemara answer the suggestion that the whole verse is about Yom Kippur?

learning.learnerQuestion: How can one verse in Leviticus 8 be the source for both the Kohen Gadol's seven-day separation and the parah adumah priest's seven-day separation?
learning.coreTension: The verse speaks of the inauguration (Rashi). Reading it as the source for two laws, the Gemara first concedes it cannot be entirely about the parah, since 'to atone' does not fit the parah; when it asks why it should not be entirely about Yom Kippur, it answers with a verbal analogy on 'tzivah' connecting the verse to the parah.
learning.coreMove: Elimination + gezerah shavah: first rule out reading the verse as about the heifer alone (since "to atone" doesn't fit the heifer), then, when a Yom-Kippur-only reading is proposed instead, use a shared word to link the verse to the heifer as well.
learning.resolution: Leviticus 8:34 is the anchor: 'to do' (parah) and 'to atone' (Yom Kippur). The gezerah shavah ('tzivah'/'tzivah' with Num 19:2) identifies 'to do' with the parah and carries the separation of 'here' (Rashi: the milu'im) over to it. The discussion continues on the next amud.

takeaway.text: Here the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' does two things: it identifies 'to do' as the parah, and it carries the separation of 'here' (Rashi: the milu'im) over to the parah.

reasoningPattern.notes: Two stages: the concession (lines 32-34) shows only that the verse cannot be read as the parah alone, and the Gemara then raises a Yom-Kippur-only reading; the Gemara answers that with the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah', which ties the verse to the parah.

learning.ahaMoment: 'To atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement, so the Gemara concedes that the whole verse cannot be the parah; to the suggestion that the whole verse is Yom Kippur, it answers with the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah'.
learning.learningBlocker: Students often read the challenge (lines 32-34) as rejecting Rabbi Yochanan's whole reading. It concedes that the verse cannot be entirely about the parah and asks only why it should not be entirely about Yom Kippur; the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers that by tying 'to do' to the parah.
learning.memoryAnchor: 'Tzivah' in the parah statute (Num 19:2) and 'tzivah' in 'as was done this day' (Lev 8:34): as there it is the parah, so here; as here there is separation, so there.

argumentFlow.label: Leviticus 8:34 split
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Manyomi bar Chilkiya, citing Rabbi Machsiya bar Idi)
argumentFlow.text: 'As was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you': 'to do' refers to the acts of the parah, and 'to atone' refers to the acts of Yom Kippur.

argumentFlow.label: But say the whole verse is about Yom Kippur
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Granted, the whole verse cannot be set on the parah, since 'to atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement. But say the whole verse is written about Yom Kippur?

argumentFlow.label: Gezerah shavah: tzivah/tzivah
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Derive it via verbal analogy: 'tzivah' in Lev 8:34 and 'tzivah' in Num 19:2 (the heifer statute). Just as there (Num 19) is the heifer, so here (Lev 8) refers to the heifer. And just as here (Lev 8) requires sequestration, so too there (Num 19) requires sequestration.

misconceptions.misconception: The gezerah shavah replaces Rabbi Yochanan's reading, so 'to atone' no longer teaches the Yom Kippur separation.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara's challenge concedes that 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. The gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers only the question about the parah, identifying 'to do' as the parah and carrying the separation of 'here' (Rashi: the milu'im) over to its kohen.

quizSeeds.question: Which verse is the source for both seven-day sequestration rules, and how does one verse teach two laws?
quizSeeds.answer: Leviticus 8:34: 'as was done this day, the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you.' 'To do' refers to the parah adumah; 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. The Gemara concedes that the whole verse cannot be the parah, since 'to atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement; when it suggests that the whole verse is about Yom Kippur, it answers with the gezerah shavah that follows.

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara answer the suggestion that Leviticus 8:34 refers only to Yom Kippur?
quizSeeds.answer: The Gemara answers with the gezerah shavah: the shared word 'tzivah' in the parah statute (Numbers 19:2) and in Leviticus 8:34 ties 'to do' to the parah, so the verse is not read as entirely about Yom Kippur.

quizSeeds.question: What two verses are linked by the gezerah shavah, and what word is shared?
quizSeeds.answer: Leviticus 8:34 ('the Lord commanded to do') and Numbers 19:2 ('this is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded'). The shared word is 'tzivah' (commanded).

prerequisiteKnowledge: Rashi: the verse refers to the milu'im (inauguration), when they were commanded to separate from their homes for seven days.
The Gemara's 'there' verse, 'this is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded', is said of the parah.

glossary.en: The name of the chamber to which the Kohen Gadol is separated from his home for the seven days before Yom Kippur.
Red Heifer. A cow burned by a priest who is sequestered seven days beforehand; the ritual is performed using dung, stone, and earth vessels, which cannot become ritually impure.

A person who immersed today and whose sun has not yet set. A tvul yom is fit for the Red Heifer; they would make the kohen who burns it tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees, who said it was performed only by those whose sun had set.

Verbal analogy. On this daf the Gemara derives 'tzivah tzivah' (lines 34-38): the word 'tzivah' (commanded) appears in 'as was done this day, the Lord commanded to do' and in 'this is the statute of the Torah which the Lord commanded'; as there it is the parah, so here it is the parah, and as here there is separation, so there there is separation.

The inauguration. Rashi explains that at the milu'im they were commanded to separate from their homes for seven days, and on the eighth day they served. Rashi reads Rabbi Yochanan's verse 'as was done this day' as referring to the milu'im.

rashiTranslations.en: "Seven days before Yom Kippur they separate the Kohen Gadol" - because the entire Yom Kippur service
is valid only when performed by the appointed High Priest, as derived in Horayot (last chapter, 12b).
Scripture says regarding Yom Kippur: "the kohen who is anointed shall make atonement" - limiting the service to the Kohen Gadol.
The Gemara (6a) explains why the separation is necessary. "To the Parhedrin chamber" - that was the chamber's name.
The Gemara explains why the chamber bore that name.
"And they prepare for him" - they designate another kohen to serve as High Priest in his place,
should some disqualifying event befall the Kohen Gadol before Yom Kippur.
The possible disqualification: a seminal emission (keri) or other impurity that bars entry to the Temple.
"And for his household" - this phrase about the Yom Kippur atonement appears in Acharei Mot.
"If so" - Rabbi Yehudah requires preparing a backup wife lest the first die before Yom Kippur.
Since he feared death - "there is no end to the matter"
Perhaps the second wife too will die - the objection stands. The Gemara now opens. "The burning of the cow" -
"of the cow" refers to the Parah Adumah (red heifer). "On the face of the Birah" - the chamber's location.
"The Birah" - the Gemara below explains what this term means.
"To the north-east" - the chamber was in the northeastern corner of the Temple courtyard.
"All its rites" of the Parah Adumah had to be performed with implements not susceptible to impurity.
"Vessels of dung" (klei gelalin) - implements made from dried cattle dung, which cannot receive impurity.
These three vessel types are explained in Menachot, in the chapter of Rabbi Yishmael.
"Vessels of earth" (klei adamah) - not kiln-fired earthenware,
but rather made from the earth itself, not fired like earthenware in a kiln.
That is, [earth] that is like soft stone, from which vessels are hollowed out.
"What is the reason" the Sages required these non-susceptible vessels for the Parah Adumah?
"Because a tevul yom is valid for the Parah Adumah" - the Gemara derives this below,
in the chapter "Taraf BaKalpi" (Yoma 43b), from the verse "and the pure one shall sprinkle."
"So that they not treat it lightly" -
people might reason: since even a tevul yom is kosher for the Parah Adumah,
perhaps there is no need to be scrupulous about its purity requirements.
Therefore the Sages imposed many rabbinic stringencies of purity upon the Parah Adumah,
and this is one of those stringencies. "Since it is a sin-offering [chatat]" -
the Parah Adumah is called a chatat, as Scripture says in Numbers 19:
"It is for purification waters, it is a sin-offering." "And a sin-offering requires the north" -
regular sin-offerings brought on the altar are slaughtered in the northern part of the courtyard.
This does not mean the Parah Adumah itself must be slaughtered in the north -
it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives, outside the Temple entirely.
"And it is written" regarding the cow (Numbers 19): "opposite the face of the Tent of Meeting" -
during the blood-sprinkling ceremony, the kohen stands on the Mount of Olives
and aims toward the entrance of the Sanctuary, which is in the eastern wall of the Temple.
"So that there be a distinguishing mark" - the northeastern chamber signals to all
that this kohen was separated there specifically for the Parah Adumah service.
The visible separation imposes the Parah Adumah service upon him formally,
since that service is called a chatat and requires an eastern orientation; the kohen must
focus his heart on performing all its rites carefully and in the correct sequence.
"The Bira which I prepared" - David's statement in Chronicles about the Temple site.
David designated the threshing-floor of Aravna the Jebusite as the site for the Temple,
and it is King David speaking this verse in Chronicles.
"From where are these matters derived?" - what is the scriptural source for the seven-day separation?
that separation is required for both Yom Kippur and the red heifer. "As he did" - just as Moses separated Aaron and his sons for seven days before the inaugural service of the Mishkan.
At the inauguration (milu'im), God commanded them to remain separated from their homes for seven days.
As Leviticus 8 states: they were to remain at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting
"day and night" - the full seven days of the inauguration period.
On the eighth day they performed the actual inaugural service, as Leviticus 9 records.
"On the eighth day [Moses] called" (Leviticus 9) and then: "approach the altar" - service followed seven days of preparation.
"As he commanded" - this pattern of seven-day separation before a major service applies to all future generations.
"To do" - to perform. The separation of seven days is required before the one-day service of Yom Kippur
"Before the performance" means: the preparatory period precedes the fulfillment of the mitzvah.
"But say [rather]" - the Gemara introduces an objection to this derivation.
